Thank you for resubmitting your article "Hippocampal low-frequency stimulation prevents seizure generation in a mouse model of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy" for consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been reviewed by John Huguenard as the Senior Editor and Reviewing Editor, and two reviewers. The following individuals involved in review of your submission have agreed to reveal their identity: Robert Hunt (Reviewer #1); Shilpa D Kadam with Brennan Sullivan (Reviewers #2).

The reviewers have discussed the reviews with one another and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this decision to help you prepare a revised submission.

We would like to draw your attention to changes in our revision policy that we have made in response to COVID-19 (https://elifesciences.org/articles/57162). Specifically, we are asking editors to accept without delay manuscripts, like yours, that they judge can stand as eLife papers without additional data, even if they feel that they would make the manuscript stronger. Thus the revisions requested below only address clarity and presentation.

Summary:

Paschen et al. show that optogenetic stimulation of medial entorhinal cortical fibers or hippocampal neurons inhibits seizures in a model of chronic temporal lobe epilepsy. Optogenetic inhibition of seizures has been described in the literature in different types of models, and targeting different cell types selectively. The experiments are performed to a very high standard, and include a painstaking and detailed characterization of the kainate model, with detailed neuropathological and in-vivo electrographic analysis of the model with different concentrations of kainate and different amounts of hippocampal damage. Different stimulus frequencies were tested for seizure control, with the most robust effects with a relatively low rate of 1 Hz.

Essential revisions:

Please see the detailed comments for your information below. The editors and reviewers agree that the following two issues need to be addressed. It is expected this should not require any additional experiments. First, please modify the text to remove any remaining claims that are not supported by statistical analysis. We think the best approach is simply to provide the quantified population results and the statistical test results. Secondly, there remains an issue of specificity of pathway stimulation. It is not entirely clear that the optogenetic approach is only affecting the MEC to DG circuit in vivo. The authors rely only on staining in the DG molecular layer as evidence of specificity. However, given the anatomy of the entorhinal-hippocampal circuit and the experimental design to target dorsal blade of DG, it would really help to show that stimulation produces no response in CA1. Alternatively, please provide images of sagittal sections documenting that virus injection was restricted to MEC, as is standard practice for these types of experiments.

Detailed comments of reviewers for this revision:

Reviewer #1:

The authors addressed almost all concerns from the prior review and added some important new data. However, I'm still not entirely convinced that the MEC to DG circuit was selectively targeted. The mCherry staining in middle molecular layer of DG is convincing, but this isn't as direct as showing successful viral targeting of only MEC (e.g., in a sagittal section). At least one animal shows mCherry staining in outer molecular layer (EP8, Figure S2). In all of the example images shown, there is also robust mCherry staining in slm of CA1 across its transverse axis. i.e., there is staining in both proximal CA1 (toward CA2) and distal CA1 (toward subiculum). MEC should preferentially project to proximal CA1 whereas LEC primarily projects to distal CA1 (Steward, 1976; Wyss, 1981; Tamamaki and Nojyo, 1995; Naber et al., 2001). Even though the pyramidal neurons are mostly lost in the epilepsy model, these mCherry-labeled MEC projections are likely synapsing onto any surviving neurons in CA1. Likewise, while it is clear that the perforant pathway is being activated in DG as the authors report, the optic fiber is extremely close to the MEC axons in CA1c (Figure S2). How do the authors know they are not activating these axons, in addition to the projections to DG?

Reviewer #2:

This is a revised submission by Paschen et al., of the manuscript entitled "Hippocampal low-frequency stimulation prevents seizure generation in a mouse model of mesial temporal lobe epilepsy" for publication in eLife. Overall, the experiments presented are of high quality and are recommended for publication. The remaining concerns are related to outstanding unsupported claims that require statistics for their inclusion in the final manuscript.

1) Frequency dependence of the LFS effects

A) Subsection “Application of different oLFS protocols during spontaneous epileptiform activity” "0.5 or 0.2 Hz also had suppressive effects on epileptiform activity, albeit less pronounced than the 1 Hz stimulation". No statistical analysis supports this statement. Figure 4P figure legend states "1Hz oLFS was the most effective stimulation frequency", however no statistical analysis supports this statement. Rather, Figure 4P demonstrates 1 and 0.5 being significantly better than 0.2, but no significant differences between 1Hz vs. 0.5Hz. This inaccuracy is also prevalent throughout the Discussion and somewhat contradictory to the logic purposed by the authors Introduction.

B) Subsection “Application of different oLFS protocols during spontaneous epileptiform activity”. "Interestingly, epileptiform activity was also suppressed in the contralateral hippocampus, with 1 Hz oLFS being most effective" No statistical analysis supports this statement, specifically "most effective".

C) Burst ratio efficacy [%] analysis was not performed for cdHC, and epileptic spike rate efficacy [%] graph is an essential analysis for cdHC and idHC.

2) Translational relevance still remains overstated.

A) The eLFS experiments demonstrate the acute effects (hours) of DBS over many weeks. These experiments are important as it demonstrates the ability for LFS to reduce epileptic activity, and the authors are commended for this work. However, the authors compare their results to clinic and to pharmacoresistance (broadly considered). This comparison is inaccurate as it does not acknowledge the limitation of analyzing anti-seizure effects over short durations of time (even if over many weeks) in their current manuscript. The authors' primary outcome of acute effects is categorically different than clinical primary outcomes (seizure diaries, continuous monitoring, etc.), and therefore such overstatements should be avoided.

B) For almost all studies cited the electrode location, frequency of stimulation, duration of stimulation, and primary outcomes were different. However, only differences in frequency parameters between studies were highlighted by the authors within the current manuscript e.g. Introduction. This is an oversimplification of the clinical data and should be revised as it is inaccurate. The closed-loop RNS system is tailored to each patient and considered a complementary therapy to anti-seizure medication, this is not reflected in the current manuscript.

C) The author's rebuttal response (point 13) and reasoning for not including female mice in their study is not reflected in the revised manuscript. This reasoning needs to be added to the methods section of the manuscript. The author's go to great lengths to compare their results to the clinic but omit female mice from their experiments, an evident contradiction.

claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of different frequencies presented in Figure 4P,Q.

claims.claim: There was no significant difference between 1 Hz and 0.5 Hz oLFS in suppressing epileptiform activity.
claims.source: whereas we found no significant difference between 1 Hz and 0.5 Hz (Figure 4P,Q; Figure 4—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison presented in Figure 4P,Q.

claims.claim: Local stimulation of DGCs via entorhinal afferents in the idHC evokes population spikes also in the cdHC.
claims.source: Local stimulation of DGCs via entorhinal afferents in the idHC evokes population spikes also in the cdHC.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by LFP recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: Population spikes occur with a latency of 8–12 ms in the cdHC relative to the population spike onsets in the idHC.
claims.source: Population spikes occur with a latency of 8–12 ms (mean ± SEM: 9 ± 0.6 ms) in the cdHC relative to the population spike onsets in the idHC.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by latency analysis presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4E.

claims.claim: Local 10 Hz photostimulation of entorhinal afferents reliably induces generalized seizures in all KA groups.
claims.source: Local 10 Hz photostimulation of entorhinal afferents reliably induces generalized seizures in all KA groups.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5A,B.

claims.claim: The time needed to induce a generalized seizure (induction time) is longer with increasing KA concentration.
claims.source: The time needed to induce a generalized seizure (induction time) is longer with increasing KA concentration.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5B showing longer induction times for 20 mM KA compared to 10 and 15 mM.

claims.claim: Mice exhibit behavioral symptoms equivalent to RS stage 1–5, independently of the KA concentration.
claims.source: Mice exhibit behavioral symptoms equivalent to RS stage 1–5, independently of the KA concentration.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: 1 Hz oLFS for 30 min before the pro-convulsive stimulus significantly decreases the seizure probability in all animals.
claims.source: 1 Hz oLFS as well as (H, I) eLFS for 30 min before the pro-convulsive stimulus significantly decreases the seizure probability in all animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5D,E.

claims.claim: eLFS for 30 min before the pro-convulsive stimulus significantly decreases the seizure probability in all animals.
claims.source: 1 Hz oLFS as well as (H, I) eLFS for 30 min before the pro-convulsive stimulus significantly decreases the seizure probability in all animals.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5H,I.

claims.claim: In trials in which seizure generalization is not prevented completely, the ensuing seizure is associated with a milder behavioral phenotype (RS).
claims.source: Trials in which seizure generalization is not prevented completely, the ensuing seizure is associated with a milder behavioral phenotype (RS).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 5F,J.

claims.claim: The cellular response to 10 Hz stimulation is reduced after 1 Hz oLFS stimulation in sessions in which seizures have been successfully suppressed.
claims.source: The response is reduced after 1 Hz oLFS stimulation in sessions in which seizures have been successfully suppressed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AUC analysis presented in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: 1 Hz oLFS was started directly after the pro-convulsive 10 Hz stimulus, ongoing seizures were not interrupted.
claims.source: When 1 Hz oLFS was started directly after the pro-convulsive 10 Hz stimulus, ongoing seizures were not interrupted (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by LFP data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Pre-conditioning with 1 Hz oLFS for 30 min prior to the pro-convulsive stimulus was highly effective in lowering the probability for seizure generalization.
claims.source: In contrast, pre-conditioning with 1 Hz oLFS for 30 min prior to the pro-convulsive stimulus was highly effective in lowering the probability for seizure generalization (Figure 5D,E, without (w/o) pre-oLFS: 91.42 ± 5.18%; with 1 Hz pre-oLFS: 14.87 ± 8.33%, p<0.001, n = 13 animals).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5D,E.

claims.claim: 0.5 Hz oLFS was also effective in preventing evoked generalized seizures.
claims.source: 0.5 Hz oLFS was also effective in preventing evoked generalized seizures (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C, w/o pre-oLFS: 97.73 ± 2.27%; with 0.5 Hz pre-oLFS: 12.12 ± 8.13%, p<0.05; n = 11 animals).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B,C.

claims.claim: Thirty minutes of 1 Hz eLFS was as effective as oLFS in reducing the probability of generalized seizures.
claims.source: Thirty minutes of 1 Hz eLFS was as effective as oLFS in reducing the probability of generalized seizures (Figure 5I, w/o pre-eLFS: 93.75 ± 6.25%; with 1 Hz pre-eLFS: 16.67 ± 9.62%) and the associated behavior (Figure 5J, w/o eLFS: RS 2.38 ± 0.40; with 1 Hz eLFS: RS 0.33 ± 0.33, n = 4 animals).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 5I,J.

claims.claim: Photostimulation (1 Hz) evoked stable response waveforms which decreased slightly in amplitude over time in non-epileptic (saline-injected) mice.
claims.source: Photostimulation (1 Hz) evoked stable response waveforms (Figure 6) which decreased slightly in amplitude over time in non-epileptic (saline-injected) mice (Figure 6A1-3, B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6A1-3,B.

claims.claim: In chronically epileptic mice, the cellular responses declined strongly and rapidly within the first 10 min during 1 Hz photostimulation.
claims.source: In chronically epileptic mice, the cellular responses declined strongly and rapidly within the first 10 min (Figure 6C1-3, D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 6C1-3,D.

claims.claim: Lower frequencies (0.5 and 0.2 Hz) altered the cellular response much less than 1 Hz.
claims.source: Lower frequencies (0.5 and 0.2 Hz) altered the cellular response much less (Figure 6E–H) as evident from AUC analysis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by AUC analysis presented in Figure 6E-H.

claims.claim: Photostimulation of afferent entorhinal fibers robustly induced depolarization of DGCs (5.1 ± 1.0 mV, n = 14 cells).
claims.source: Photostimulation of afferent entorhinal fibers robustly induced depolarization of DGCs (5.1 ± 1.0 mV, n = 14 cells) and was occasionally sufficient to induce action potentials (−70 mV holding potential, n = 4 cells).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recording data from acute slices.

claims.claim: During oLFS, evoked synaptic responses were strongly depressed (reduction of EPSP amplitude to 28.5 ± 9.9% of the original response, n = 14 cells).
claims.source: During oLFS, evoked synaptic responses were strongly depressed (Figure 7B, reduction of excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) amplitude to 28.5 ± 9.9% of the original response, n = 14 cells).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recording data presented in Figure 7B.

claims.claim: In non-sclerotic control slices (saline mice), oLFS for 10 min reduced the discharge probability of DGCs.
claims.source: In non-sclerotic control slices (saline mice), oLFS for 10 min reduced the discharge probability of DGCs (Figure 7C, number of action potentials generated per trial at 100 V stimulation, no-oLFS: 1.8 ± 0.5 vs. after oLFS: 0.24 ± 0.15, p<0.05, n = 11 cells).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell-attached recording data presented in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: DGCs were overall more excitable in KA mice compared to control mice.
claims.source: Although DGCs were overall more excitable in KA mice, as reported previously in this model (Janz et al., 2017a), the number of action potentials in response to electrical stimulation was significantly reduced upon 10 min oLFS (Figure 7D, number of action potentials generated per trial at 100 V stimulation, no-oLFS: 3.5 ± 0.6 vs. after oLFS: 2.1 ± 0.5, p<0.05, n = 19 cells).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Janz et al., 2017a and data presented in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: The number of action potentials in response to electrical stimulation was significantly reduced upon 10 min oLFS in KA mice.
claims.source: the number of action potentials in response to electrical stimulation was significantly reduced upon 10 min oLFS (Figure 7D, number of action potentials generated per trial at 100 V stimulation, no-oLFS: 3.5 ± 0.6 vs. after oLFS: 2.1 ± 0.5, p<0.05, n = 19 cells).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by cell-attached recording data presented in Figure 7D.

claims.claim: Intrinsic properties of DGCs in KA mice were not altered by the applied stimulation protocol.
claims.source: In contrast, intrinsic properties of DGCs in KA mice were not altered by the applied stimulation protocol (control: resting membrane potential (Vm) = −73.4 ± 1.1 mV; Cm = 53.5 ± 3.7 pF; Rm = 298.7 ± 27.4 MΩ; Rheobase = 150.8 ± 14.1 pA; n = 27 cells; after oLFS: Vm = −74.8 ± 1.3 mV; Cm = 56.4 ± 7.5 pF; Rm = 313.9 ± 36.8 MΩ; Rheobase = 153.3 ± 26.4 pA; n = 14 cells).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by whole-cell recording data showing no significant changes in intrinsic properties.

claims.claim: KA-treated mice have strongly reduced inhibition in the sclerotic hippocampus which is most likely due to the loss of inhibitory interneurons.
claims.source: Additionally, we measured spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) of DGCs in slices of control and epileptic mice and confirmed that KA-treated mice have strongly reduced inhibition in the sclerotic hippocampus which is most likely due to the loss of inhibitory interneurons (Figure 7E, sIPSCs frequency: saline 3.9 ± 0.5 Hz vs. KA 0.4 ± 0.2 Hz, p<0.05, n = 5 cells; sIPSCs amplitude: saline 24.0 ± 2.1 pA vs. KA 80.4 ± 15.2 pA, p<0.05, n = 4 cells, all at +20 mV).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sIPSC recording data presented in Figure 7E and inference about the cause.

claims.claim: During 2 weeks of daily eLFS, spontaneous epileptiform activity was successfully suppressed in each eLFS session but returned to reference level during the following 2 hr.
claims.source: During these 2 weeks, spontaneous epileptiform activity was successfully suppressed in each eLFS session but returned to reference level during the following 2 hr (Figure 8B–G, Figure 8—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by repeated LFP recording data presented in Figure 8B-G.

claims.claim: Compared to the first reference recording, epileptiform activity remained unchanged in the intermittent reference recordings.
claims.source: Compared to the first reference recording, epileptiform activity remained unchanged in the intermittent reference recordings (Figure 8H, Figure 8—source data 1; Figure 8J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by reference LFP data presented in Figure 8H,J.

claims.claim: 3 hr continuous eLFS effectively reduces the high-load burst ratio over the whole stimulation period, reoccurring in a lower manner within 1 hr after stimulation.
claims.source: 3 hr continuous eLFS effectively reduces the high-load burst ratio over the whole stimulation period, reoccurring in a lower manner within 1 hr after stimulation (Two-way ANOVA; Tukey's multiple comparison test ***p<0.001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8I.

claims.claim: An initial 30 min eLFS and 10 min 'on-off' stimulation protocol abolishes epileptic spikes during the stimulation cycle.
claims.source: An initial 30 min eLFS and 10 min 'on-off' stimulation protocol abolishes epileptic spikes during the stimulation cycle.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8K,L.

claims.claim: Approximately 40 min after the last 10 min eLFS the epileptic spike rate starts to rise again.
claims.source: Approximately 40 min after the last 10 min eLFS the epileptic spike rate starts to rise again.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 8K,L.

claims.claim: Mice with a misplaced stimulation electrode showed no reduction of the high-load burst ratio.
claims.source: Interestingly, mice with a misplaced stimulation electrode (i.e. not in the dentate gyrus, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A, n = 3) showed no reduction of the high-load burst ratio (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B, pre: 0.16 ± 0.02; eLFS: 0.15 ± 0.03; post 1: 0.15 ± 0.02; post 2: 0.17 ± 0.03; n = 3 animals)
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by control data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Mice with a misplaced stimulation electrode showed only a slight reduction of the epileptic spike rate during eLFS.
claims.source: and only a slight reduction of the epileptic spike rate during eLFS (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C, pre: 0.59 ± 0.05 Hz; eLFS: 0.43 ± 0.05 Hz; post 1: 0.60 ± 0.06; post 2: 0.71 ± 0.10; pre vs. eLFS p<0.01; n = 3 animals).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by control data presented in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: The stimulation target, i.e. the dentate gyrus, is important for a successful seizure interference in the intrahippocampal KA mouse model.
claims.source: This suggests that the stimulation target, i.e. the dentate gyrus, is important for a successful seizure interference in the intrahippocampal KA mouse model (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of correctly and incorrectly placed electrodes.

claims.claim: Different KA concentrations resulted in variable degrees of histopathological changes and the development of spontaneous recurrent epileptiform activity.
claims.source: We found that different KA concentrations resulted in variable degrees of histopathological changes and the development of spontaneous recurrent epileptiform activity as previously described for 20 mM KA injection (Janz et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figures 2 and 3, and a citation to Janz et al., 2017b.

claims.claim: Cell death of hilar neurons increased with the KA dose, whereas DGCs survived equally but dispersed more strongly.
claims.source: In particular, cell death of hilar neurons increased with the KA dose, whereas DGCs survived equally but dispersed more strongly.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 2.

claims.claim: GCD appeared to be related to the amount of cell loss in the hilus in human patients.
claims.source: This is in line with previous reports from human patients, showing that GCD appeared to be related to the amount of cell loss in the hilus (Houser, 1990) and that DGCs survive in the sclerotic tissue (Thom, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Houser, 1990 and Thom, 2014.

claims.claim: DGCs survive in the sclerotic tissue in human patients.
claims.source: This is in line with previous reports from human patients, showing that GCD appeared to be related to the amount of cell loss in the hilus (Houser, 1990) and that DGCs survive in the sclerotic tissue (Thom, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thom, 2014.

claims.claim: The sclerotic hippocampus in the intrahippocampal KA mouse model is thought to be critically involved in seizure generation.
claims.source: Similar to the human pathology, the sclerotic hippocampus in the intrahippocampal KA mouse model is thought to be critically involved in seizure generation (Krook-Magnuson et al., 2015; Pallud et al., 2011; Walker, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Krook-Magnuson et al., 2015, Pallud et al., 2011, and Walker, 2015.

claims.claim: Epileptiform activity generated in the sclerotic focus often spreads to the contralateral hippocampus in MTLE patients.
claims.source: Epileptiform activity generated in the sclerotic focus often spreads to the contralateral hippocampus in MTLE patients (Gloor et al., 1993; Mintzer et al., 2004) and KA-treated mice (Janz et al., 2018; Meier et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies in patients and mice.

claims.claim: Epileptiform activity propagated less frequently to the contralateral hippocampus in mice with strong hippocampal sclerosis, than in those with mild sclerosis.
claims.source: We observed that epileptiform activity propagated less frequently to the contralateral hippocampus in mice with strong hippocampal sclerosis, than in those with mild sclerosis, pointing toward a relationship between network preservation and seizure spread.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3 and represents an inference about the relationship between sclerosis severity and seizure spread.

claims.claim: Following KA injection, CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells are extensively lost.
claims.source: Following KA injection, CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells are extensively lost (Bouilleret et al., 1999; Marx et al., 2013), whereas DGCs and their entorhinal afferents are preserved (Janz et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bouilleret et al., 1999 and Marx et al., 2013.

claims.claim: DGCs and their entorhinal afferents are preserved following KA injection.
claims.source: Following KA injection, CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells are extensively lost (Bouilleret et al., 1999; Marx et al., 2013), whereas DGCs and their entorhinal afferents are preserved (Janz et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Janz et al., 2017a.

claims.claim: By positioning the optic fiber above the molecular layer of the dentate gyrus, the study stimulated mainly the perforant path.
claims.source: Accordingly, by positioning the optic fiber as precisely as possible above the molecular layer of the dentate gyrus, we stimulated mainly the perforant path (Janz et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Janz et al., 2018 and the experimental design.

claims.claim: CA2 neurons, surviving CA3 pyramidal cells, or temporoammonic fibers were most likely not activated by light delivery.
claims.source: Hence, CA2 neurons, surviving CA3 pyramidal cells, or temporoammonic fibers (in cases of mild hippocampal sclerosis) were most likely not activated by light delivery.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the positioning of the optic fiber and the restricted light penetration.

claims.claim: 1 Hz oLFS was identified as a highly effective stimulation frequency to suppress spontaneous epileptiform activity in the sclerotic and also in the undamaged, contralateral hippocampus.
claims.source: Using this experimental design, we identified 1 Hz oLFS as a highly effective stimulation frequency to suppress spontaneous epileptiform activity in the sclerotic and also in the undamaged, contralateral hippocampus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: LFS at 1 Hz has been used previously to alleviate epileptiform activity in vitro.
claims.source: LFS at 1 Hz has been used previously to alleviate epileptiform activity. In vitro approaches showed that optogenetic activation of calcium/calmodulin-dependent protein kinase type II (CaMKII)-positive neurons for 3 min in the entorhinal cortex and electrical stimulation of the ventral hippocampal commissure for 15 min disrupt seizure-like activity induced by 4-Aminopyridine (4-AP) (Shiri et al., 2017; Toprani and Durand, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shiri et al., 2017 and Toprani and Durand, 2013.

claims.claim: Electrical 1 Hz stimulation of Schaffer collaterals in acute hippocampal slices for 10 min diminished epileptiform activity induced by bicuculline.
claims.source: Also, electrical 1 Hz stimulation of Schaffer collaterals in acute hippocampal slices for 10 min diminished epileptiform activity induced by bicuculline (Albensi et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Albensi et al., 2004.

claims.claim: Long-term effects of 1 Hz LFS over several hours were reported from in vivo studies using amygdala kindling or pilocarpine rodent models.
claims.source: In addition to this short-term efficacy of 1 Hz LFS, long-term effects over several hours (60 min continuous stimulation or alternating periods of 15 min on/off for 4 hr) were reported from in vivo studies using amygdala kindling or pilocarpine rodent models targeting the ventral hippocampal commissure or entorhinal cortex (Rashid et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rashid et al., 2012 and Xu et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Most optogenetic studies decreased network activity either by direct inhibition of hippocampal principal cells or by activating GABAergic interneurons.
claims.source: Most optogenetic studies decreased network activity either by direct inhibition of hippocampal principal cells or by activating GABAergic interneurons (Kokaia et al., 2013; Krook-Magnuson et al., 2013; Ladas et al., 2015; Ledri et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple optogenetic studies.

claims.claim: Optogenetic stimulation of mossy cells in the dorsal dentate gyrus can control electrographic seizures, but the effect was much weaker than with direct inhibition of DGCs.
claims.source: More recently, Bui et al., 2018 showed that optogenetic stimulation of mossy cells in the dorsal dentate gyrus can control electrographic seizures, but the effect was much weaker than with direct inhibition of DGCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bui et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Local 1 Hz photostimulation of entorhinal afferents effectively suppressed epileptiform activity in both hippocampi independent of the severity of hippocampal sclerosis.
claims.source: Accordingly, local 1 Hz photostimulation of entorhinal afferents effectively suppressed epileptiform activity in both hippocampi independent of the severity of hippocampal sclerosis.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Lower stimulation frequencies (0.5 and 0.2 Hz) were less effective than 1 Hz.
claims.source: Lower stimulation frequencies (0.5 and 0.2 Hz) were less effective.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4.

claims.claim: LFS is not effective in inducing synaptic depression in sclerotic human hippocampal slices.
claims.source: Supporting this notion, LFS is not effective in inducing synaptic depression in sclerotic human hippocampal slices (Beck et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beck et al., 2000.

claims.claim: LFS drives the hippocampal network into a stable state, reducing the probability of seizures while LFS is ongoing.
claims.source: Concerning acute seizure-suppressive effects, we suggest that LFS drives the hippocampal network into a stable state, reducing the probability of seizures while LFS is ongoing.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claims.claim: Evoked interictal-like discharges elicit anti-epileptic effects, contingent on the network state as well as stimulus amplitude and frequency.
claims.source: This hypothesis is supported by Chang et al., 2018 who showed that evoked interictal-like discharges elicit anti-epileptic effects, contingent on the network state as well as stimulus amplitude and frequency.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: oLFS of entorhinal afferents may introduce glutamatergic synaptic perturbation followed by transient suppression of neuronal activity.
claims.source: In line with this interpretation, oLFS of entorhinal afferents may introduce glutamatergic synaptic perturbation followed by transient suppression of neuronal activity (de Curtis et al., 2001; de Curtis and Avanzini, 2001; Muldoon et al., 2015) and thus may interfere with recurrent generation of epileptiform activity (Chang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Curtis et al., 2001, de Curtis and Avanzini, 2001, Muldoon et al., 2015, and Chang et al., 2018.

claims.claim: LFS improved cognitive function in pilocarpine-injected rats.
claims.source: However, Wang et al., 2020 demonstrated that LFS improved cognitive function in pilocarpine-injected rats.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2020.

claims.claim: 1 Hz LFS in the dentate gyrus is a highly efficient approach to interfere with seizure generation in the MTLE mouse model with hippocampal sclerosis.
claims.source: In conclusion, our study identified 1 Hz LFS in the dentate gyrus as a highly efficient approach to interfere with seizure generation in the MTLE mouse model with hippocampal sclerosis.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: The effect of LFS was largely driven by repetitive activation of DGCs residing in the sclerotic seizure focus.
claims.source: We demonstrated that the effect was largely driven by repetitive activation of DGCs residing in the sclerotic seizure focus, and we have shed light on the associated cellular mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results, particularly from the slice experiments.

claims.claim: The findings may pave the way for effective seizure control in one of the most common forms of drug-resistant epilepsy.
claims.source: Considering the potential for clinical translation, our findings may pave the way for effective seizure control in one of the most common forms of drug-resistant epilepsy.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential clinical implications of the findings.

claims.claim: Experiments were conducted with adult (8–12 weeks) transgenic male mice (C57BL/6-Tg(Thy1-eGFP)-M-Line).
claims.source: Experiments were conducted with adult (8–12 weeks) transgenic male mice (C57BL/6-Tg(Thy1-eGFP)-M-Line) (Feng et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects used in the study.

claims.claim: In total, 96 mice were used for this study.
claims.source: In total, 96 mice were used for this study.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the sample size of the study.

claims.claim: All animal procedures were carried out under the guidelines of the European Community's Council Directive of September 22, 2010 (2010/63/EU) and were approved by the regional council (Regierungspräsidium Freiburg).
claims.source: All animal procedures were carried out under the guidelines of the European Community's Council Directive of September 22, 2010 (2010/63/EU) and were approved by the regional council (Regierungspräsidium Freiburg).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the study.

claims.claim: Mice were injected with KA or saline into the right dorsal hippocampus.
claims.source: Mice were injected with KA or saline into the right dorsal hippocampus (KA: n = 53, saline: n = 5 for in vivo experiments and KA: n = 34, saline: n = 4 for acute slice electrophysiology), as described previously (Heinrich et al., 2006; Häussler et al., 2012; Janz et al., 2017a).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure with citations to previous studies.

claims.claim: Mice that did not have SE or died due to KA treatment or surgical procedures were excluded from further experiments.
claims.source: Mice that did not have SE (n = 5) or died due to KA treatment (n = 18) or surgical procedures (n = 2) were excluded from further experiments.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about exclusion criteria for the study.

claims.claim: For optogenetic stimulation of entorhinal fibers, KA- and saline-treated animals were stereotaxically injected with a recombinant adeno-associated virus (AAV) carrying the genomic sequences for ChR2 fused to mCherry under the control of the CaMKIIa promoter into the ipsilateral medial entorhinal cortex.
claims.source: For optogenetic stimulation of entorhinal fibers, KA- and saline-treated animals were stereotaxically injected with a recombinant adeno-associated virus (AAV, 0.45 µl; n = 50 for in vivo experiments and n = 28 for acute slice electrophysiology), carrying the genomic sequences for ChR2 fused to mCherry under the control of the CaMKIIa promoter (AAV1.CaMKIIa.hChR2(H134R)-mCherry.WPRE.hGH; Penn Vector Core, Pennsylvania, USA) into the ipsilateral medial entorhinal cortex in the same surgery (Janz et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for viral injection.

claims.claim: For in vivo experiments Teflon-coated platinum-iridium wires were implanted 16 days after injections at three hippocampal positions: ipsilateral dorsal (idHC), ipsilateral ventral (ivHC) and contralateral dorsal (cdHC).
claims.source: For in vivo experiments Teflon-coated platinum-iridium wires (125 µm diameter; World Precision Instruments, Sarasota, Florida, USA) were implanted 16 days after injections at three hippocampal positions as described previously (Janz et al., 2018): ipsilateral dorsal (idHC), ipsilateral ventral (ivHC) and contralateral dorsal (cdHC).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for electrode implantation.

claims.claim: All animals were additionally implanted with an optic fiber in the same position as the idHC electrode, but at a 30° angle.
claims.source: All animals were additionally implanted with an optic fiber (ferrule 1.25 mm, cannula 200 µm diameters; Prizmatix Ltd., Givat-Shmuel, Israel) in the same position as the idHC electrode, but at a 30° angle.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for optic fiber implantation.

claims.claim: For electrical stimulation, 11 animals received an additional electrode (coated with nanostructured platinum), in parallel to the optic fiber.
claims.source: For electrical stimulation, 11 animals received an additional electrode (coated with nanostructured platinum [Boehler et al., 2020]), in parallel to the optic fiber.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for electrical stimulation electrode implantation.

claims.claim: Three mice had to be excluded due to wrong electrode positions.
claims.source: Three mice had to be excluded due to wrong electrode positions (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about exclusion criteria based on histological verification.

claims.claim: After recovery from implantations, the freely behaving mice were first recorded on 2 successive days (3 hr each) to determine reference LFPs.
claims.source: After recovery from implantations, the freely behaving mice were first recorded on 2 successive days (3 hr each) to determine reference LFPs (Figure 1).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for baseline recordings.

claims.claim: On days 21–28 after KA and virus injection, photostimulation with pulsed blue light (460 nm; 50 ms pulse duration; 150 mW/mm² at the fiber tip) was applied at low frequencies (1, 0.5, or 0.2 Hz) to test the effect of oLFS on spontaneous epileptiform activity.
claims.source: On days 21–28 after KA and virus injection (10, 15, or 20 mM KA, AAV1.CamKIIa.ChR2-mCherry), photostimulation with pulsed blue light (460 nm; 50 ms pulse duration; 150 mW/mm² at the fiber tip; blue LED, Prizmatix Ltd.) was applied at low frequencies (1, 0.5, or 0.2 Hz) to test the effect of oLFS on spontaneous epileptiform activity.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure for optogenetic stimulation.

claims.claim: The radius of light emission with sufficient power to activate ChR2 did not exceed 500 µm.

results.result: The manuscript provides background on MTLE, establishing it as the most common form of focal, pharmacoresistant epilepsy in adults, often associated with hippocampal sclerosis characterized by neuronal cell loss, gliosis, granule cell dispersion, and mossy fiber sprouting. Surgical resection is effective for many patients but not suitable for those with multiple foci or at risk of resection-related impairments.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C8-C13 are well-supported by citations to established literature (Engel 2001, Blümcke et al. 2013, Thom 2014, Englot and Chang 2014) and represent accepted knowledge in the field. These background claims appropriately contextualize the study.

results.result: The authors establish that deep brain stimulation (DBS) at high frequencies (130-200 Hz) is currently used for intractable seizures, but its efficacy is variable in MTLE patients with hippocampal sclerosis. Low-frequency stimulation (LFS) at 5 Hz has shown effectiveness in small cohort studies and would be favorable for clinical implementation due to lower power requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C20 are supported by appropriate citations to clinical literature (Li and Cook 2018, Boëx et al. 2011, Velasco et al. 2007, Koubeissi et al. 2013, Lim et al. 2016). The rationale for investigating LFS as an alternative to HFS is well-established based on prior clinical observations.

results.result: The authors justify their experimental model choice by noting that optogenetic approaches have been successful in rodent MTLE models but typically target pyramidal cells or GABAergic interneurons, which are diminished in hippocampal sclerosis. The intrahippocampal kainate (KA) model replicates major hallmarks of human MTLE pathology while preserving dentate granule cells (DGCs) and their entorhinal inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C25 are well-supported by citations to relevant literature (Krook-Magnuson and Soltesz 2015, Zhao et al. 2015, Bouilleret et al. 1999, Froriep et al. 2012, Janz et al. 2017a, Häussler et al. 2016). The rationale for targeting preserved DGCs rather than lost cell populations is sound.

results.result: The authors modified the intrahippocampal KA mouse model by using three different KA concentrations (10, 15, and 20 mM) to achieve variable degrees of hippocampal sclerosis. Higher KA concentrations (15 and 20 mM) resulted in greater hilar cell loss and granule cell dispersion compared to 10 mM, while CA1 pyramidal cell loss and Gad67+ interneuron loss were similar across groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28, C30-C31, C74-C75 are supported by quantitative histological data presented in Figure 2 with appropriate statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post-hoc test, p<0.001 for significant differences). Sample sizes are stated (n=4, 6, 5 animals for 10, 15, 20 mM groups). The correlation between KA dose and pathological severity is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Epileptiform activity occurred in both hippocampi of all KA mice, with the ipsilateral dorsal hippocampus (idHC) of 10 mM KA mice showing a smaller percentage of high-load bursts compared to 15 or 20 mM groups. The extent of granule cell dispersion and hilar cell loss was positively correlated with the high-load burst ratio in the idHC (Pearson's r = 0.84, p<0.0001 for GCD; r = 0.64, p<0.01 for hilar cell loss).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C36 are supported by LFP recording data presented in Figure 3 with appropriate statistical analysis and correlation tests. The automated burst classification algorithm (described in C144-C150) provides objective quantification. The strong correlation between pathological severity and epileptiform activity validates the model modification.

results.result: Optogenetic low-frequency stimulation (oLFS) at 1 Hz for 1 hour effectively suppressed spontaneous epileptiform activity in both the ipsilateral and contralateral hippocampi, independent of KA concentration. Lower frequencies (0.5 and 0.2 Hz) were less effective, with 1 Hz significantly more effective than 0.2 Hz but not significantly different from 0.5 Hz. No effect was observed in no-virus controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C42, C85, C91-C92 are supported by comprehensive LFP data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1 with appropriate statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA with Dunn's multiple comparison test). The frequency-dependent effect is clearly demonstrated, and proper controls (no-virus) are included. Sample sizes are adequate across all KA concentrations.

results.result: Local optogenetic stimulation of entorhinal afferents in the ipsilateral dorsal hippocampus (idHC) evoked population spikes in the contralateral dorsal hippocampus (cdHC) with a latency of 8-12 ms (mean ± SEM: 9 ± 0.6 ms), suggesting polysynaptic propagation.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C44 are supported by detailed analysis of LFP recordings presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 4, including latency measurements that remained stable over 1 hour of stimulation. The polysynaptic delay is consistent with interhippocampal propagation and helps explain bilateral seizure suppression from unilateral stimulation.

results.result: Local 10 Hz photostimulation of entorhinal afferents reliably induced generalized seizures in all KA groups, with longer induction times for higher KA concentrations (20 mM: 13.67 ± 1.86 s vs. 10 mM: 5.75 ± 0.63 s, p<0.01). Mice exhibited behavioral symptoms equivalent to Racine stages 1-5 independent of KA concentration.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are supported by data in Figure 5A-C with appropriate statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA with Tukey's post-hoc test). The inverse relationship between sclerosis severity and seizure induction time is interesting and well-documented. Behavioral scoring using the established Racine scale adds rigor.

results.result: Preconditioning with 1 Hz oLFS for 30 minutes before a pro-convulsive 10 Hz stimulus was highly effective in preventing seizure generalization (seizure probability reduced from 91.42 ± 5.18% to 14.87 ± 8.33%, p<0.001, n=13 animals). Preconditioning with 0.5 Hz oLFS was also effective (seizure probability reduced from 97.73 ± 2.27% to 12.12 ± 8.13%, p<0.05, n=11 animals).
results.evaluation: Claims C48, C53-C54 are supported by data in Figure 5D-E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B-C with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon rank test). The dramatic reduction in seizure probability with preconditioning is a key finding. Sample sizes are adequate and effect sizes are large.

results.result: Electrical low-frequency stimulation (eLFS) at 1 Hz for 30 minutes was as effective as oLFS in reducing the probability of generalized seizures (from 93.75 ± 6.25% to 16.67 ± 9.62%) and associated behavioral symptoms (Racine stage from 2.38 ± 0.40 to 0.33 ± 0.33, n=4 animals).
results.evaluation: Claims C49 and C55 are supported by data in Figure 5H-J, but the sample size is small (n=4 animals) and no statistical test results are reported for the eLFS preconditioning experiments. While the effect appears similar to oLFS, the lack of statistical analysis and small sample size limit confidence in this conclusion.

results.result: In trials where seizure generalization was not completely prevented by preconditioning LFS, the ensuing seizures were associated with milder behavioral phenotypes (lower Racine stages).
results.evaluation: Claim C50 is supported by behavioral data in Figure 5F and 5J showing significant reductions in Racine stage scores (Wilcoxon rank test, p<0.001 for oLFS, n=13 animals). This demonstrates a dose-response relationship where partial suppression still provides clinical benefit.

results.result: The cellular response to 10 Hz stimulation (measured as area under the curve, AUC) was reduced by approximately 40% after 1 Hz oLFS preconditioning in sessions where seizures were successfully suppressed (AUC: 266.9 ± 53.89 without oLFS vs. 139.2 ± 19.08 with oLFS, p<0.01, n=11 animals).
results.evaluation: Claim C51 is supported by AUC analysis presented in Figure 5G with appropriate statistical testing (paired t-test, p<0.01). The reduction in evoked response amplitude provides a mechanistic link between LFS preconditioning and seizure prevention, though the exact mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: When 1 Hz oLFS was started directly after the pro-convulsive 10 Hz stimulus (on-demand approach), ongoing seizures were not interrupted.
results.evaluation: Claim C52 is supported by LFP data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A showing that oLFS applied after seizure onset does not terminate the seizure. This negative result is important for understanding the timing requirements of LFS intervention and distinguishes preconditioning from on-demand approaches.

results.result: During 1 Hz photostimulation, evoked response waveforms in non-epileptic mice decreased slightly over time, while in chronically epileptic mice, cellular responses declined strongly and rapidly within the first 10 minutes. Lower frequencies (0.5 and 0.2 Hz) altered cellular responses much less than 1 Hz.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are supported by in vivo LFP data presented in Figure 6 showing frequency-dependent changes in evoked response amplitudes over time. The AUC analysis provides quantitative support. However, the mechanisms underlying these differential responses are not fully elucidated.

results.result: In acute slice experiments, photostimulation of entorhinal fibers induced robust depolarization of DGCs (5.1 ± 1.0 mV, n=14 cells). During 10 minutes of 1 Hz oLFS, evoked synaptic responses were strongly depressed (EPSP amplitude reduced to 28.5 ± 9.9% of original, n=14 cells), and discharge probability was significantly reduced in both control (1.8 ± 0.5 to 0.24 ± 0.15 APs/trial, p<0.05, n=11 cells) and KA mice (3.5 ± 0.6 to 2.1 ± 0.5 APs/trial, p<0.05, n=19 cells).
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C61, C63 are supported by whole-cell and cell-attached patch-clamp recordings from acute slices presented in Figure 7 with appropriate statistical analysis. The slice experiments provide crucial mechanistic insights into how LFS reduces network excitability. Sample sizes are adequate for electrophysiology experiments.

results.result: DGCs were overall more excitable in KA mice compared to control mice, as reported previously in this model.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 is supported by a citation to Janz et al. 2017a and is consistent with the higher baseline discharge probability shown in Figure 7D (3.5 ± 0.6 APs/trial in KA vs. 1.8 ± 0.5 in control). This validates the epileptic phenotype of the model.

results.result: Intrinsic properties of DGCs in KA mice (resting membrane potential, capacitance, membrane resistance, rheobase) were not altered by the 10-minute oLFS stimulation protocol.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 is supported by whole-cell recording data showing no significant changes in intrinsic properties before and after oLFS (n=27 control cells, n=14 after oLFS). This suggests that LFS effects are mediated by synaptic rather than intrinsic mechanisms, though statistical tests are not explicitly reported for these comparisons.

results.result: KA-treated mice have strongly reduced inhibition in the sclerotic hippocampus (sIPSC frequency: 3.9 ± 0.5 Hz in saline vs. 0.4 ± 0.2 Hz in KA, p<0.05; sIPSC amplitude: 24.0 ± 2.1 pA in saline vs. 80.4 ± 15.2 pA in KA, p<0.05), which is most likely due to the loss of inhibitory interneurons.
results.evaluation: Claim C65 is supported by sIPSC recording data in Figure 7E with appropriate statistical analysis (Mann-Whitney test, p<0.05). The reduced frequency and increased amplitude of sIPSCs are consistent with interneuron loss shown histologically (C30). The inference about causation is reasonable but not definitively proven.

results.result: During 2 weeks of daily 1 Hz eLFS (1 hour per day), spontaneous epileptiform activity was successfully suppressed in each session but returned to reference levels within 2 hours post-stimulation. Epileptiform activity remained unchanged in intermittent reference recordings compared to the first reference recording.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by repeated LFP recording data over 2 weeks presented in Figure 8B-H with appropriate statistical analysis. The stability of both the suppressive effect during stimulation and the baseline activity between sessions demonstrates the reproducibility and lack of desensitization over time.

results.result: Three hours of continuous eLFS effectively reduced the high-load burst ratio over the entire stimulation period, with activity reoccurring at a lower level within 1 hour after stimulation (two-way ANOVA with Tukey's multiple comparison test, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claim C68 is supported by data in Figure 8I with appropriate statistical analysis. The extended stimulation period demonstrates that the suppressive effect can be maintained for longer durations, which is important for clinical translation.

results.result: An intermittent stimulation protocol (initial 30 min eLFS followed by four cycles of 10 min off/10 min on) abolished epileptic spikes during the stimulation cycle, with the epileptic spike rate starting to rise again approximately 40 minutes after the last 10-minute eLFS.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are supported by data in Figure 8K-L showing that discontinuous stimulation can maintain seizure suppression. This is clinically relevant as it could reduce power consumption and potential side effects. However, the sample size and number of replicates are not clearly stated for this experiment.

results.result: Mice with misplaced stimulation electrodes (not in the dentate gyrus, n=3) showed no reduction in high-load burst ratio and only a slight reduction in epileptic spike rate during eLFS (pre: 0.59 ± 0.05 Hz vs. eLFS: 0.43 ± 0.05 Hz, p<0.01), suggesting that the dentate gyrus is an important target for successful seizure interference.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C73 are supported by control data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 showing minimal effects with off-target stimulation. This anatomical specificity control strengthens the conclusion that DGC activation is critical for the observed effects. However, the sample size is small (n=3) and the inference about mechanism (C73) is reasonable but not definitive.

results.result: The authors contextualize their findings by noting that in human MTLE patients, granule cell dispersion is related to hilar cell loss, DGCs survive in sclerotic tissue, the sclerotic hippocampus is critically involved in seizure generation, and epileptiform activity often spreads to the contralateral hippocampus. They observed that epileptiform activity propagated less frequently to the contralateral hippocampus in mice with strong sclerosis than in those with mild sclerosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C80 are supported by appropriate citations to human and animal studies (Houser 1990, Thom 2014, Krook-Magnuson et al. 2015, Pallud et al. 2011, Walker 2015, Gloor et al. 1993, Mintzer et al. 2004, Janz et al. 2018, Meier et al. 2007) and by data in Figure 3 showing the relationship between sclerosis severity and contralateral spread.

results.result: Following KA injection, CA1 and CA3 pyramidal cells are extensively lost while DGCs and their entorhinal afferents are preserved. By positioning the optic fiber above the molecular layer of the dentate gyrus, the study stimulated mainly the perforant path, with CA2 neurons, surviving CA3 pyramidal cells, or temporoammonic fibers most likely not activated.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 are supported by citations to previous studies (Bouilleret et al. 1999, Marx et al. 2013, Janz et al. 2017a, 2018) and by the experimental design shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2. The estimation of light penetration (C113) supports the inference about spatial specificity, though some off-target activation cannot be completely ruled out.

results.result: The authors place their work in context by noting that 1 Hz LFS has been used previously to alleviate epileptiform activity in vitro and in vivo in various models, and that most optogenetic studies decreased network activity by inhibiting principal cells or activating GABAergic interneurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C90 are supported by appropriate citations to prior literature (Shiri et al. 2017, Toprani and Durand 2013, Albensi et al. 2004, Rashid et al. 2012, Xu et al. 2016, Kokaia et al. 2013, Krook-Magnuson et al. 2013, Ladas et al. 2015, Ledri et al. 2014, Bui et al. 2018). This contextualizes the novelty of their approach.

results.result: LFS is not effective in inducing synaptic depression in sclerotic human hippocampal slices.
results.evaluation: Claim C93 is supported by a citation to Beck et al. 2000. This is used to argue against synaptic depression as the sole mechanism of LFS effects in their model, though the authors acknowledge that some synaptic depression does occur in their experiments.

results.result: The authors propose that LFS drives the hippocampal network into a stable state, reducing seizure probability while ongoing. This hypothesis is supported by work showing that evoked interictal-like discharges elicit anti-epileptic effects contingent on network state, stimulus amplitude, and frequency. They suggest oLFS may introduce glutamatergic synaptic perturbation followed by transient suppression of neuronal activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 represent mechanistic hypotheses supported by citation to Chang et al. 2018 and other studies (de Curtis et al. 2001, de Curtis and Avanzini 2001, Muldoon et al. 2015). While the proposed mechanisms are plausible and consistent with the data, they remain speculative and would require additional experiments to definitively test.

results.result: LFS improved cognitive function in pilocarpine-injected rats.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 is supported by citation to Wang et al. 2020. This is mentioned to address potential concerns about LFS impairing hippocampal function, though the authors acknowledge that future research will need to address this question in their specific model.

results.result: The authors conclude that 1 Hz LFS in the dentate gyrus is a highly efficient approach to interfere with seizure generation in the MTLE mouse model with hippocampal sclerosis. They demonstrate that 1 Hz LFS for 1 hour resulted in almost complete suppression of spontaneous seizures in both hippocampi, this effect remained stable over several weeks of daily stimulation, 30 minutes of LFS before a pro-convulsive stimulus prevented seizure generalization, and acute slice experiments revealed reduced efficacy of perforant path transmission onto granule cells. The effect was largely driven by repetitive activation of DGCs in the sclerotic seizure focus, and the findings may pave the way for effective seizure control in drug-resistant epilepsy.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7, C98-C100 represent the main conclusions of the study and are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data presented throughout the manuscript (Figures 4-8). The multi-level approach (in vivo LFP recordings, behavioral assessments, acute slice electrophysiology) provides converging evidence. The conclusion about clinical translation potential (C100) is appropriately cautious ("may pave the way") given that this is a preclinical study.

results.result: The methods section describes the experimental procedures including animal subjects (adult male transgenic mice, n=96 total), KA and virus injections, electrode and optic fiber implantations, optogenetic and electrical stimulation protocols, and recording session designs. Appropriate ethical approvals were obtained, and exclusion criteria are clearly stated.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C128 describe the experimental methods in detail with appropriate citations to previous studies for established procedures. The methods appear rigorous with clear descriptions of stereotaxic coordinates, stimulation parameters, and session designs. Exclusion criteria are transparent (C105, C110, C143). However, some details about randomization and blinding are limited.

results.result: The methods section describes tissue preparation, histological procedures (FISH, immunohistochemistry), image acquisition, and quantitative analysis of hippocampal sclerosis. Masking was performed for histological quantification, with the evaluator unaware of KA treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C142 describe histological methods with appropriate detail and citations to established protocols (Kulik et al. 2003, Schindelin et al. 2012). The inclusion of blinding (C137) for histological analysis is a strength. The quantification methods for GCD, cell loss, and interneuron counts are clearly described and appear appropriate.

results.result: The methods section describes the automated analysis of epileptiform activity using a custom algorithm (Heining et al. 2019) that detects spikes, groups them into bursts, extracts feature vectors, and classifies bursts using a self-organizing map (SOM) into low-, medium-, and high-load categories. The high-load burst ratio was calculated as the fraction of time spent in high-load bursts. Automatic detection was confirmed by visual inspection.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C154 describe the computational analysis methods with appropriate citation to the algorithm development (Heining et al. 2019). The use of an automated, objective classification system is a strength. Visual confirmation of automated detection (C151) adds validation. Exclusion criteria for low-activity sessions (C152) are clearly stated. However, details about algorithm validation and inter-rater reliability are limited.

results.result: The methods section describes acute slice electrophysiology procedures including slice preparation with NMDG-based protective solution, whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in the presence of GABAA and GABAB receptor blockers, extracellular stimulation protocols, and photostimulation parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C160 describe electrophysiology methods with appropriate detail and citation to previous work (Elgueta et al. 2015). The use of NMDG-based protective solution for slice preparation is a modern best practice. Recording conditions and stimulation parameters are clearly specified. The methods appear rigorous and reproducible.

results.result: Statistical analyses were performed using Prism 8 software with appropriate tests for different comparisons: paired or unpaired Student's t-test for two groups, one-way or two-way ANOVA with Tukey's post-hoc test for multiple groups, REML for missing values, and Pearson's correlation for correlations. Significance thresholds were set at p<0.05, p<0.01, and p<0.001.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C166 describe statistical methods that appear appropriate for the types of data and comparisons made. The use of REML for missing data (C164) is appropriate. However, there is no mention of corrections for multiple comparisons across the many tests performed, which could inflate Type I error rates. Sample sizes vary across experiments and are not always clearly justified.
